sentences.text: For four days they were on the Salar.
They stayed at the salt lodge, and each morning they drove out to a different part of the flat, and Elena took pictures.
She used the second roll on the second day.
She used the third roll on the third day.

Ernesto had driven to the small town of Uyuni and bought her two more rolls at a shop he knew, and she used those too, more slowly, aware now that film was finite in a way she had not quite understood on the first afternoon.
Ernesto did not photograph.
He watched her.
He carried water for her, and made her wear her sunhat, and made her rest in the shade of the jeep in the middle of each day.
He watched her walk out onto the mirror and become a small dark figure in the enormous whiteness, camera up to her face.
He watched her sit cross-legged in the shallow water for half an hour once, waiting for a cloud to move exactly where she wanted it.
He watched her hand her the camera to Don Juan one evening, and Don Juan look through the viewfinder at her framing and nod, seriously, and hand it back.
He was, for those four days, the happiest he had been in years, and it took him a while to notice this.
On the fifth morning, their last, they went out early — before dawn, so they could be on the Salar when the light came up.
It was cold and dark when they parked the jeep.
Elena walked out onto the flat in her rubber boots.
Ernesto walked behind her.
The light began to lift in the east, and the enormous mirror began to fill with soft pink, then gold, then finally the pale blue of full morning.
Elena took perhaps twenty photographs.
Then she stopped.
She turned around and looked at her father, standing ten paces behind her in his grey poncho, and she walked back to him.
She held the camera out.
She said, "Papi.
One picture.
Of me." Ernesto looked at the camera in her hands.
He did not move for a moment.
Then he took it.
He said, "One?" She said, "Yes.
Just one.
Where I stand now.
In the middle of the mirror.
So I have a photograph of me from the Salar.
And you have taken it."
Ernesto walked back to where he had been.
Elena walked out to where she wanted to stand.
She stopped.
She lifted her arms very slightly, not posing exactly, just — being there.
She looked at her father.
He raised the camera to his eye.
He took a long time.
He was framing it very carefully.

He was looking at his daughter through the viewfinder for the first time in his life, and he was, Elena could tell even from that distance, taking a long slow moment to be there and to make the picture.
Then he pressed the shutter.
There was a small clean click.
He lowered the camera.
He walked back to her.
He handed her the camera.
He said, "I do not know how it will turn out.
I have not done this in thirty years.
But I did it."
Elena took the camera back.
She said, "It will turn out.
I know it will."
They drove home the next two days.
The Salar receded behind them and became one more thing that had happened.
Elena kept the camera case in her lap the whole drive.
Ernesto did not push her to talk.
She thought a lot.
She looked out at the altiplano, and at the vicuñas in the distance, and at the mountains, and she thought.
About halfway home she said, "Papi.
If I take pictures for the rest of my life, will you always not?" Ernesto thought about this for a long time.
Then he said, "I do not know, mi hija.
I have not decided.
What I know is that I took one picture on the Salar last week.
And I remember it exactly.
I can close my eyes and see the frame.
That is different from anything I have taken in thirty years.
Maybe I will take one picture a year now.
Or one picture a trip.
Not many.
Just — the ones I really want to make.
When I know why.
I will not become a photographer.
But I will not throw away the camera anymore."
Three weeks after they got home, they took the five rolls of film to a small photo shop in La Paz.
It was one of the last shops in the city that still developed film.
The owner remembered Ernesto from years ago and asked, with mild surprise, whether Ernesto had taken up photography.
Ernesto laughed and said no — his daughter had.
The shop took a week to develop the rolls.
When Elena went back with her father to collect them, the owner handed her five thick envelopes of prints, plus the negatives in translucent sleeves.
They opened the envelopes at the kitchen table in the apartment.
Elena's mother came over from the stove to look.
Elena spread the prints out — a hundred and seventy or so photographs, taken by a ten-year-old on a five-day trip.
Some were blurry.
Some were badly framed.
But some were extraordinary.
There was one, taken lying on her back on the mirror, that showed the sky in every direction with only the small silhouette of a bird at the edge.
There was one of Don Juan's coffee cup sitting on the salt-brick table at the lodge.
There was one of the mountains floating, and one of her father's boots reflected upside down.
And near the end of the third roll, in the middle of Elena's series from the fifth morning, was one photograph that was not by Elena.
It showed her — small, in her red poncho, arms slightly raised, standing in the middle of the mirror in the soft golden light, framed by the sky above and the sky below.
Her mother picked it up and looked at it for a long time.
She said, "Ernesto.
Who took this?" Ernesto did not say anything.
Elena said, "Papi did.
It is the only picture he took.
In thirty years."
Elena's mother put the photograph down very gently in the middle of the table.
She looked at Ernesto.
She did not say anything either.
But she smiled a small smile that Elena had not seen before, and she went back to the stove.
And Elena took the photograph and put it, later, above her small desk in her bedroom, where she could see it when she was doing her homework.
She would keep it there for the rest of her life.

And her father, though nobody said this at the time, would take one more photograph the next February, and one more the next, and one more the next, all of her, all of them, all of them of the way she looked at things — a small quiet series that nobody but the two of them would ever know had begun with a single frame at the edge of a mirror at the end of the world.
